docs.title: thinking.py
docs.text:
Source: utils/thinking.py

Following the prompt serialization and template loading mechanisms detailed in prompts.py, the thinking.py module governs cognitive resource allocation and reasoning effort budgets across all Large Language Model (LLM) interaction points. Where prompts.py ensures structural integrity of inputs and outputs, thinking.py regulates the computational depth and latency profile of the inference requests dispatched across the pipeline.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
utils/thinking.py implements the per-node thinking effort resolution subsystem, referred to internally as "thinking flows." Modern reasoning LLMs—such as Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Google Gemini 2.5 / 3.x, and reasoning models served through OpenRouter—support variable reasoning parameters (such as thinking_budget, thinking_level, or reasoning_effort). Because different compilation phases within Codebase-Knowledge-Builder require radically different reasoning depth, applying a uniform reasoning level across the entire execution graph results in excessive API latency, token exhaustion, or degraded architectural synthesis. The module solves this optimization challenge by mapping individual pipeline call sites to an ordered cognitive effort scale.

The architecture operates on a three-tier hierarchy of precedence resolved once during application bootstrap in main.py: 1. Per-node Overrides (--thinking-override NODE=LEVEL): Explicit granular overrides assigned to specific call sites via command-line flags. 2. Global Effort Level (--thinking-level LEVEL): A uniform override applied across every node in the pipeline. 3. Preset Profiles (--thinking-profile PROFILE): Predefined effort allocation tables (economy, balanced, quality, max, off) that assign calibrated effort levels based on node sensitivity, modified dynamically by execution mode (tutorial, advanced, sdk, api-reference).

The module standardizes effort along an ordered canonical scale: minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. Reasoning-heavy structural discovery phases (such as identify_abstractions and reduce_abstractions) receive high-tier allocations, whereas mechanical tasks (such as filter_files or translate_strings) are assigned minimal or low effort. Provider drivers (llm_anthropic.py, llm_gemini.py, and llm_openrouter.py) translate canonical project levels into provider-specific parameters at dispatch time using nearest-neighbor fallback resolution.

docs.title: resolve_profile_name()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def resolve_profile_name(profile: str | None, provider: str | None) -> str:

Description: Resolves the operational profile identifier against the active model provider. When an explicit profile name (such as "economy", "balanced", "quality", or "max") is provided, the function normalizes the string to lowercase and returns it. If the profile is omitted or specified as "auto", the function evaluates whether the target provider is an explicitly profiled ecosystem (ANTHROPIC, GEMINI, or OPENROUTER). In those ecosystems, current foundation models reason by default and per-node calibration is a vital cost-control mechanism, causing "auto" to resolve to "balanced". For generic or local endpoints (such as Ollama or OpenAI-compatible hosts), "auto" defaults to "off", preserving model-native behavior.

Parameters: * profile (str | None): The requested profile name passed via configuration or CLI flags. Defaults to "auto" if None. * provider (str | None): The uppercase identifier of the target inference provider (e.g., "ANTHROPIC", "GEMINI", "OPENROUTER", "OLLAMA").

Returns: * str: The normalized, concrete profile identifier ("balanced", "off", or the explicitly supplied profile).

Raises: * This function does not raise exceptions; unexpected or unmapped profile names pass through normalized.

Example: 

def resolve_profile_name(profile: str | None, provider: str | None) -> str:
    """Resolve `auto` to a concrete profile for the active provider."""
    profile = (profile or "auto").lower()
    if profile == "auto":
        return "balanced" if provider in PROFILED_PROVIDERS else "off"
    return profile

The implementation performs a single-pass fallback check. By decoupling provider identification from CLI argument ingestion, it enables upstream initialization routines to establish operational profiles before driver instantiation. Providers outside PROFILED_PROVIDERS default to "off", preventing downstream payload injectors from sending unsupported reasoning keys to third-party OpenAI-compatible REST endpoints.

docs.title: clamp_level()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def clamp_level(level: str, supported) -> str | None:

Description: Normalizes an abstract project reasoning level to an explicit level supported by a specific model target. The function searches the target model's supported capabilities against the canonical THINKING_LEVELS tuple. If the exact level is directly supported, it returns unchanged. If the requested level is unsupported, the function identifies all overlapping supported levels and computes the nearest neighbor on the THINKING_LEVELS index scale. In the event of an equidistant tie between two supported levels, the algorithm deterministically selects the lower effort tier, safeguarding token budgets. If the model supports no recognized levels, or if the input level is not present in THINKING_LEVELS, it returns None.

Parameters: * level (str): The requested reasoning level string (e.g., "high", "xhigh", "minimal"). * supported (Iterable[str]): A collection or container (such as a set, list, or tuple) containing the thinking levels officially supported by the active model or provider catalog.

Returns: * str | None: The exact level, the closest supported level ranked along the scale (ties breaking toward lower effort), or None if no valid level can be resolved.

Raises: * This function does not raise exceptions.

Example: 

def clamp_level(level: str, supported) -> str | None:
    """Return `level` if the model supports it, else the nearest supported level on
    THINKING_LEVELS (ties → lower). None when nothing on the scale is supported."""
    if level in supported:
        return level
    ranked = [lvl for lvl in THINKING_LEVELS if lvl in supported]
    if not ranked or level not in THINKING_LEVELS:
        return None
    target = THINKING_LEVELS.index(level)
    return min(ranked, key=lambda lvl: (abs(THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl) - target), THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl)))

The clamping logic uses an absolute index distance metric paired with the index value as a secondary sorting key: (abs(THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl) - target), THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl)). This tuple comparison guarantees that if a requested level (e.g., index 2) is flanked symmetrically by supported levels at index 1 and index 3, the secondary element breaks the tie by choosing index 1. This prevents vendor drivers such as llm_gemini.py or llm_openrouter.py from failing request schema validation when models only advertise a subset of reasoning modes (e.g., only "low" and "high").

docs.title: parse_overrides()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def parse_overrides(values: list[str] | None) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:

Description: Parses and validates raw command-line override parameters passed via --thinking-override flags. The function processes a list of key-value assignment strings formatted as NODE=LEVEL. Each entry is split at the first delimiter, stripped of surrounding whitespace, and normalized to lowercase. It verifies that the parsed node name exists within NODE_KEYS and that the assigned level exists within THINKING_LEVELS. Valid entries are aggregated into an overrides dictionary, while malformed strings or unknown tokens are collected into an invalid values list for consolidated error reporting by the CLI runner.

Parameters: * values (list[str] | None): A list of command-line override strings, typically sourced from sys.argv via argparse. Accepts None gracefully.

Returns: * tuple[dict[str, str], list[str]]: A 2-tuple containing: 1. overrides: A dictionary mapping valid node keys (str) to valid thinking levels (str). 2. invalid: A list of original string values (str) that failed delimiter parsing, contained invalid node names, or specified unrecognized levels.

Raises: * This function does not raise exceptions directly; syntax and schema validation errors are returned as structured data.

Example: 

def parse_overrides(values: list[str] | None) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:
    """Parse NODE=LEVEL strings. Returns (overrides, invalid_values)."""
    overrides, invalid = {}, []
    for value in values or []:
        node, sep, level = value.partition("=")
        node, level = node.strip().lower(), level.strip().lower()
        if not sep or node not in NODE_KEYS or level not in THINKING_LEVELS:
            invalid.append(value)
        else:
            overrides[node] = level
    return overrides, invalid

The implementation relies on str.partition("=") rather than str.split("=") to guarantee safe single-split execution without throwing ValueError on missing delimiters. The guard clause validates three critical conditions: presence of the separator, membership of the node in NODE_KEYS, and validity of the assigned level in THINKING_LEVELS. By returning invalid values rather than halting execution, the function allows main.py to report every syntax error in a single terminal diagnostic emission before execution begins.

docs.title: build_thinking_plan()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def build_thinking_plan(profile: str, mode: str, global_level: str | None, overrides: dict) -> dict:

Description: Synthesizes the master thinking execution plan mapping every known node key in NODE_KEYS to a resolved thinking level or None. The construction enforces a strict precedence hierarchy: CLI overrides override global level overrides, which in turn override baseline profile allocations. When a global_level is defined, every node key is initialized to that uniform level. When no global level is specified, the plan initializes from _PROFILES using the resolved profile name and applies mode-specific adjustments from _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS. If the profile is "off", every node is initialized to None, directing inference drivers to omit explicit reasoning payloads and accept vendor defaults. Finally, all keys present in the overrides dictionary are merged into the plan, taking ultimate precedence.

Parameters: * profile (str): The pre-resolved profile name (e.g., "balanced", "economy", "quality", "max", "off"). * mode (str): The operational documentation mode ("tutorial", "advanced", "sdk", "api-reference"). * global_level (str | None): An optional uniform thinking level assigned across all pipeline nodes via --thinking-level. * overrides (dict[str, str]): A validated dictionary of per-node overrides returned by parse_overrides().

Returns: * dict[str, str | None]: A complete mapping of every string key in NODE_KEYS to its assigned thinking level (str) or None.

Raises: * This function does not raise exceptions directly.

Example: 

def build_thinking_plan(profile: str, mode: str, global_level: str | None, overrides: dict) -> dict:
    """Return {node_key: level | None} for every NODE key.

    Precedence: overrides > global_level > profile table (+ mode adjustments).
    `profile` must already be resolved (see resolve_profile_name).
    """
    if global_level:
        plan = dict.fromkeys(NODE_KEYS, global_level.lower())
    elif profile in _PROFILES:
        plan = dict(_PROFILES[profile])
        plan.update(_MODE_ADJUSTMENTS.get(profile, {}).get(mode, {}))
    else:  # "off": every node uses the model's default thinking behavior
        plan = dict.fromkeys(NODE_KEYS)
    plan.update(overrides)
    return plan

This function ensures that the resulting plan dictionary is fully populated across all known NODE_KEYS. When global_level is set, profile definitions and mode adjustments are bypassed entirely. When relying on profiles, _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS handles task nuances—such as elevating chapter writing in "advanced" mode under the "economy" profile from "low" to "medium" to accommodate architectural trade-off synthesis. Merging overrides at the final step ensures explicit CLI instructions cannot be overwritten by mode or profile heuristics.

docs.title: resolve_thinking_level()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def resolve_thinking_level(shared: dict, node_key: str) -> str | None:

Description: Resolves the runtime thinking level for a specific LLM execution site during graph node execution. It inspects the pipeline state dictionary (shared) for a compiled "thinking_plan" dictionary. If the plan exists and contains node_key, its assigned level is returned. If no plan is present or the key is absent, the function falls back defensively to the top-level "thinking_level" key stored in the shared state. If neither exists, it returns None.

Parameters: * shared (dict): The central shared context dictionary passed across execution nodes in flow.py and nodes.py. * node_key (str): The unique string identifier of the active execution node (must match an entry in NODE_KEYS).

Returns: * str | None: The resolved thinking level string (e.g., "medium", "high"), or None if the node should execute using model defaults.

Raises: * This function does not raise exceptions.

Example: 

def resolve_thinking_level(shared: dict, node_key: str) -> str | None:
    """Thinking level for one LLM call site. Falls back to the global level when no plan exists."""
    plan = shared.get("thinking_plan")
    if plan and node_key in plan:
        return plan[node_key]
    return shared.get("thinking_level")

This helper abstracts the pipeline state lookup across all call sites in nodes.py. Graph nodes invoke this function immediately prior to dispatching prompts to call_llm.py. Because the returned string is vendor-agnostic, downstream dispatchers remain decoupled from the workflow state schema, delegating final parameter mapping to provider drivers.

docs.title: describe_plan()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def describe_plan(plan: dict, mode: str | None = None) -> str:

Description: Generates a compact, single-line human-readable summary of a thinking plan for terminal startup telemetry and diagnostic logging. It restricts output exclusively to nodes relevant to the active operational mode (using MODE_NODES), preventing terminal clutter from unused pipeline phases. If a node maps to None or an empty value, it renders as "default".

Parameters: * plan (dict[str, str | None]): The compiled thinking plan mapping node keys to levels. * mode (str | None): The operational documentation mode ("tutorial", "advanced", "sdk", "api-reference"). If omitted or invalid, formatting falls back to evaluating all keys in NODE_KEYS.

Returns: * str: A comma-separated string of key=level assignments (e.g., "filter_files=low, write_chapters=high, chapter_summary=low").

Raises: * This function does not raise exceptions.

Example: 

def describe_plan(plan: dict, mode: str | None = None) -> str:
    """Compact one-line rendering for the startup config display (only nodes that run in `mode`)."""
    keys = MODE_NODES.get(mode, NODE_KEYS)
    return ", ".join(f"{key}={plan.get(key) or 'default'}" for key in keys)

The helper filters execution nodes by consulting MODE_NODES.get(mode, NODE_KEYS). In "api-reference" mode, for instance, structural discovery nodes like map_abstractions and reduce_abstractions are omitted from startup logs since the deterministic 1:1 file mapper bypasses those workflow steps. The fallback expression plan.get(key) or 'default' ensures unconfigured or "off" nodes are legibly labeled in CLI startup banners.

docs.title: Internal Helpers
docs.text: The thinking.py module defines no private helper functions or nested closures. All algorithmic operations are exposed directly through the public API functions documented above. Internal state is maintained through module-scoped constant collections (_ANALYSIS_NODES, _PROFILES, and _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS) that isolate configuration tables from external mutation.

docs.title: THINKING_LEVELS
docs.text:
An ordered tuple defining the standardized reasoning scale across the application: 

THINKING_LEVELS = ("minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")
* Type: tuple[str, ...] * Purpose: Serves as the canonical coordinate space for effort comparisons and distance calculations in clamp_level(). While minimal is reserved for select OpenRouter endpoints, shipped profiles restrict standard baselines to low, medium, high, xhigh, and max.

docs.title: THINKING_PROFILES
docs.text:
An immutable tuple enumerating all recognized profile identifiers: 

THINKING_PROFILES = ("auto", "off", "economy", "balanced", "quality", "max")
* Type: tuple[str, ...] * Purpose: Used for CLI argument validation and documentation.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The module employs defensive normalization and graceful degradation rather than raising runtime exceptions:

  • Safe Delimiter Splitting: parse_overrides() uses str.partition("=") to separate arguments without risking ValueError on strings lacking an = separator. It verifies each token against NODE_KEYS and THINKING_LEVELS before accepting it into the plan, collecting malformed entries into an invalid list so callers can emit descriptive terminal diagnostics.
  • Nearest-Neighbor Fallback: clamp_level() guards against API rejection when a model lacks support for an assigned level. Rather than throwing an error or failing payload validation, it uses distance minimization across THINKING_LEVELS indices to select the closest available level. Equidistant ties break toward the lower level to prevent unexpected billing spikes.
  • Defensive Property Access: resolve_thinking_level() uses dict.get() across nested dictionaries, falling back gracefully to the global thinking_level or None if the thinking plan is uninitialized.
  • Safe Profile Fallback: resolve_profile_name() treats None as "auto", defaulting unrecognized providers to "off" to prevent sending invalid parameters to unsupported REST endpoints.

docs.title: token_utils.py
docs.text: Source: utils/token_utils.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
Operating downstream from the cognitive allocation framework established in thinking.py—which assigns granular reasoning budgets across pipeline execution nodes—token_utils.py serves as the centralized token calculation, context sizing, and prompt capacity management engine for the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder architecture. Large-scale codebase analysis tasks require prompt packing near context ceilings, creating risks of prompt truncation, silent buffer overflow, or API rejections due to unreserved output space. This module isolates the mechanics of token counting, model-specific token ratio scaling, context window resolution, and telemetry logging to ensure pipeline nodes operate safely within provider boundaries.

The component interfaces directly with OpenAI's tiktoken library using the cl100k_base BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) tokenizer as a reference metric. Because importing vendor-specific tokenizers (such as Anthropic Claude or Google Gemini tokenizers) introduces heavy native dependencies and latency overhead, token_utils.py pairs tiktoken with calibrated scaling multipliers sourced from llm_config.py via get_token_ratio(). For resilience against missing native C-bindings or system architecture incompatibilities, the module incorporates a deterministic fallback heuristic (len(text) // 4). Context window bounds are dynamically computed through provider-aware reservation algorithms: models sharing unified prompt-and-output contexts reserve planned thinking and completion space alongside flat margins, while decoupled architectures (such as Google Gemini) apply isolated margins.

Telemetry and operational visibility are integrated directly into prompt sizing operations. The module interfaces with output.py and Python's standard logging infrastructure to emit real-time token capacity metrics, styled ANSI console warnings, and structured log records detailing prompt payload compositions. This telemetry allows upstream pipeline drivers in nodes.py and flow.py to audit memory consumption and token distributions before initiating model inference.

docs.title: resolve_max_tokens()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def resolve_max_tokens(shared: dict) -> int:

Description: Resolves the maximum context window token limit for the current execution cycle. It first checks the shared workflow dictionary for an explicitly configured "max_tokens" override. If no override exists, it queries the active LLM provider configuration via resolve_llm_settings() and resolves the context window length using get_model_context_length(). It records a debug entry to the persistent log via emit_raw() before returning the integer limit.

Parameters: * shared (dict): The central execution state dictionary shared across pipeline workflow nodes, potentially containing runtime user overrides.

Returns: * int: The maximum token limit of the active model context window.

Raises: * Does not explicitly raise exceptions; errors encountered during configuration resolution propagate from llm_config.py.

Example: 

def resolve_max_tokens(shared):
    """Resolve max_tokens from shared store or auto-detect from the active provider."""
    max_tokens = shared.get("max_tokens")
    if max_tokens is not None:
        return max_tokens
    _, model_name, endpoint, api_key = resolve_llm_settings()
    max_tokens_val = get_model_context_length(endpoint, model_name, api_key)
    from utils.output import emit_raw

    emit_raw("DEBUG", f"resolve_max_tokens | resolved max_tokens={max_tokens_val:,}", dest="LOG")
    return max_tokens_val

The function prioritizes values present in the pipeline's runtime dictionary, enabling user-supplied CLI flags or test harnesses to constrain model contexts deterministically. When falling back to automatic detection, it coordinates settings resolution without modifying the shared dictionary in place, maintaining pure read-only semantics. Sourcing the context ceiling directly from catalog lookups prevents hardcoded limit drift across vendor updates.

docs.title: input_token_budget()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def input_token_budget(max_tokens: int, thinking_level: str | None = None) -> int:

Description: Calculates the maximum permissible prompt size (in count_tokens() units) that guarantees adequate context space for model generation and reasoning traces. For unified context architectures (Anthropic and OpenRouter), it reserves the planned output tokens derived from context_output_reserve() plus CONTEXT_MARGIN. For separated context architectures (such as Google Gemini) or unrecognized providers, it reserves 5% of the total context window clamped between 8,192 and 64,000 tokens. The function enforces an absolute minimum floor of half the total context window (max_tokens // 2).

Parameters: * max_tokens (int): The total context window limit of the target model. * thinking_level (str | None, optional): The reasoning effort intensity (e.g., "low", "medium", "high") applied to the request. Defaults to None.

Returns: * int: The maximum token count available for the input prompt payload.

Raises: * Does not raise exceptions.

Example: 

def input_token_budget(max_tokens: int, thinking_level: str | None = None) -> int:
    """Largest prompt size (in count_tokens() units) that still leaves room for the response."""
    planned = context_output_reserve(thinking_level)
    if planned is not None:
        reserve = planned + CONTEXT_MARGIN
    else:
        reserve = min(max(int(max_tokens * 0.05), MIN_OUTPUT_RESERVE), MAX_OUTPUT_RESERVE)
    return max(max_tokens - reserve, max_tokens // 2)

The algorithm dynamically accounts for vendor-specific architectural differences in token management. Anthropic Claude and OpenRouter models share a single memory pool across input prompt, chain-of-thought tokens, and emitted text, necessitating an explicit reservation that accommodates thinking depth. In contrast, Google Gemini models isolate input ceilings from output limits, requiring only the static margin. Clamping the fallback reserve between MIN_OUTPUT_RESERVE (8,192 tokens) and MAX_OUTPUT_RESERVE (64,000 tokens) protects large-context models from excessively large reserves while preserving room on smaller models.

docs.title: count_tokens_raw()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def count_tokens_raw(text: str) -> int:

Description: Computes the baseline token count of a given string using tiktoken's cl100k_base BPE encoding. To prevent parsing failures on source code payloads containing special substrings, it explicitly sets disallowed_special=(). If tiktoken is unavailable or fails to initialize, the function falls back to a standard integer division heuristic (len(text) // 4).

Parameters: * text (str): The raw text or source code payload to evaluate.

Returns: * int: The raw estimated token count without provider-specific ratio adjustments.

Raises: * Does not raise exceptions; all internal initialization and encoding errors fallback to character heuristics.

Example: 

def count_tokens_raw(text: str) -> int:
    """Count tokens with tiktoken (cl100k_base), with fallback to chars/4. No model calibration."""
    if not text:
        return 0
    enc = _get_encoding()
    if enc:
        return len(enc.encode(text, disallowed_special=()))
    return len(text) // 4

This function forms the uncalibrated token counting baseline for the application. Setting disallowed_special=() is critical when processing code repositories, as identifiers such as <|endoftext|> or custom prompt markers would otherwise trigger an immediate DisallowedSpecialToken exception from tiktoken. Returning 0 for falsy or empty strings prevents downstream calculations from executing redundant encoding routines.

docs.title: count_tokens()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:

Description: Estimates the token footprint for a string tailored to the active model family. It first calculates the raw BPE token count using count_tokens_raw() and then scales the result by the ratio retrieved from llm_config.get_token_ratio(). The ratio is resolved once and cached in the module singleton _token_ratio.

Parameters: * text (str): The text or prompt content to measure.

Returns: * int: The calibrated token estimate reflecting the active model's tokenization density.

Raises: * Does not raise exceptions.

Example: 

def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    """Estimate tokens for the active model: tiktoken count x llm_config.get_token_ratio() (per model family)."""
    global _token_ratio
    raw = count_tokens_raw(text)
    if not raw:
        return 0
    if _token_ratio is None:
        _token_ratio = get_token_ratio()
    return int(raw * _token_ratio) if _token_ratio != 1.0 else raw

Because different model families employ distinct token vocabularies (e.g., Anthropic's Claude tokenizer yields different token densities than OpenAI's cl100k_base on dense programming languages), direct raw counts can underestimate prompt size. By caching _token_ratio as a module singleton, this function avoids repeated configuration parsing across the thousands of token counting passes executed during codebase indexing.

docs.title: log_token_estimation()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def log_token_estimation(node_name: str, prompt_content: str, max_tokens: int, token_usage: dict | None = None) -> None:

Description: Computes prompt capacity metrics, formats sub-component usage breakdowns, and dispatches telemetry to both the interactive terminal and structured log files.

Parameters: * node_name (str): The identifier of the executing pipeline graph node (e.g., "draft_chapters", "map_abstractions"). * prompt_content (str): The assembled prompt string to measure. * max_tokens (int): The maximum context window ceiling used to calculate capacity percentage. * token_usage (dict | None, optional): An optional dictionary mapping prompt sub-component labels to their respective token counts. Defaults to None.

Returns: * None

Raises: * Does not raise exceptions; handles division-by-zero defensively if max_tokens or token_count is zero.

docs.title: Phase 1: Capacity Calculation
docs.text:
token_count = count_tokens(prompt_content)
    percentage = (token_count / max_tokens) * 100 if max_tokens else 0
The first phase evaluates the calibrated token count of the prompt payload using count_tokens(). It then computes the percentage of total model capacity consumed by the prompt, defensively guarding against division by zero if max_tokens is passed as 0.

docs.title: Phase 2: Usage Breakdown Formatting
docs.text:
# Build token usage breakdown suffix for stdout display
    suffix = ""
    usage_log_str = ""
    if token_usage:
        max_label_len = max(len(label) for label in token_usage)
        lines = []
        log_parts = []
        for label, value in token_usage.items():
            pct = (value / token_count * 100) if token_count else 0
            padded_label = label.ljust(max_label_len)
            lines.append(f"\t{padded_label} : {value:,} ({pct:.0f}%)")
            log_parts.append(f"{label}={value:,} ({pct:.0f}%)")
        suffix = "\n" + "\n".join(lines)
        usage_log_str = " | " + " | ".join(log_parts)
When a token_usage mapping is provided, the function aligns labels using ljust() based on the longest key length. For each component, it computes the fraction of total prompt tokens consumed and builds two distinct string representations: a multi-line, tab-indented suffix for human-readable terminal rendering, and a compact, pipe-delimited segment string for flat log file persistence.

docs.title: Phase 3: Telemetry Dispatch
docs.text:
# Console output via emit (styled by CSV LEVEL=WARNING → yellow)
    emit(
        "TOKEN_ANALYTICS",
        suffix=suffix,
        node_name=node_name,
        token_count=f"{token_count:,}",
        max_tokens=f"{max_tokens:,}",
        percentage=f"{percentage:.1f}",
    )

    # File log stays single-line for parseability (structured, not translatable)
    logger.info(f"NODE EXEC | node={node_name} | prompt_tokens={token_count:,} / {max_tokens:,} ({percentage:.1f}% capacity){usage_log_str}")
The final phase emits telemetry across two segregated channels. It calls emit() using the "TOKEN_ANALYTICS" event key to display formatted output to the terminal, and writes a single-line structured record containing prompt tokens, context limits, capacity percentage, and sub-breakdowns to logger.info().

docs.title: _get_encoding()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _get_encoding() -> tiktoken.Encoding | None:

Description: Lazily loads and returns the singleton tiktoken encoding instance for cl100k_base. If the encoding has not yet been initialized, it attempts retrieval inside an exception guard. If initialization fails due to missing byte-pair encoding data files or environment constraints, _encoding is set to None and cached to bypass repeated import overhead on subsequent invocations.

Parameters: * None

Returns: * tiktoken.Encoding | None: The initialized cl100k_base tokenizer instance, or None if initialization failed.

Raises: * Does not raise exceptions; all errors during encoding acquisition are trapped and handled.

Example: 

def _get_encoding():
    global _encoding
    if _encoding is None:
        try:
            _encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
        except Exception:
            _encoding = None
    return _encoding

Lazy instantiation eliminates startup latency during pipeline bootstrap when token counting may not be immediately required. Catching generic Exception ensures that environments lacking internet access or local cache access for tiktoken BPE files fail gracefully to heuristic estimation rather than terminating the pipeline.

docs.title: Module Singletons and Limits
docs.text:

MAX_OUTPUT_RESERVE int Public Constant Upper bound on fallback output reservations, set to 64_000 tokens. _encoding tiktoken.Encoding \| None Private State Cached singleton holding the active cl100k_base encoding object. _token_ratio float \| None Private State Cached scaling multiplier mapping raw tiktoken counts to target model counts.

docs.title: Structured Log Record Format
docs.text:
File-backed audit logs written to logger.info() conform to a standardized, single-line format:

NODE EXEC | node=<node_name> | prompt_tokens=<count> / <limit> (<percentage>% capacity)[ | <label>=<count> (<pct>%) ...]

Example output: 

NODE EXEC | node=identify_abstractions | prompt_tokens=14,250 / 128,000 (11.1% capacity) | System Prompt=850 (6%) | File Tree=13,400 (94%)

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The module implements defensive design patterns to guarantee that token sizing and logging errors never crash upstream synthesis nodes:

  • Tokenizer Initialization Protection: In _get_encoding(), any runtime failure (such as network unavailability or missing BPE assets) is caught via except Exception:. The module sets _encoding = None and silently falls back to character division heuristic estimation (len(text) // 4).
  • Special Token Escaping: count_tokens_raw() invokes enc.encode(text, disallowed_special=()), preventing unescaped control tokens in ingested source files (e.g., <|endoftext|>, <|fim_prefix|>) from triggering runtime tokenization exceptions.
  • Division-by-Zero Guards: log_token_estimation() guards all percentage calculations with conditional fallbacks (... if max_tokens else 0 and ... if token_count else 0), preventing ZeroDivisionError when measuring empty strings or uninitialized model contexts.
  • Context Reservation Floor Bounds: input_token_budget() enforces max(max_tokens - reserve, max_tokens // 2). If output reservations and safety margins exceed the total context window, the prompt budget is guaranteed at least 50% of the model ceiling, preventing negative budget calculations.
